verses.text: In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams; and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep went from him.
Then the king commanded to call the magicians, and the enchanters, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, to tell the king his dreams. So they came in and stood before the king.
The king said to them, I have dreamed a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know the dream.
Then spoke the Chaldeans to the king in the Syrian language, O king, live forever: tell your servants the dream, and we will show the interpretation.
The king answered the Chaldeans, The thing is gone from me: if you don’t make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you shall be cut in pieces, and your houses shall be made a dunghill.
But if you show the dream and its interpretation, you shall receive of me gifts and rewards and great honor: therefore show me the dream and its interpretation.
They answered the second time and said, Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will show the interpretation.
The king answered, I know of a certainty that you would gain time, because you see the thing is gone from me.

But if you don’t make known to me the dream, there is but one law for you; for you have prepared lying and corrupt words to speak before me, until the time be changed: therefore tell me the dream, and I shall know that you can show me its interpretation.

The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said, There is not a man on the earth who can show the king’s matter, because no king, lord, or ruler, has asked such a thing of any magician, or enchanter, or Chaldean.
It is a rare thing that the king requires, and there is no other who can show it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh.
For this cause the king was angry and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise men of Babylon.
So the decree went out, and the wise men were to be slain; and they sought Daniel and his companions to be slain.
Then Daniel returned answer with counsel and prudence to Arioch the captain of the king’s guard, who was gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon;
he answered Arioch the king’s captain, Why is the decree so urgent from the king? Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel.
Daniel went in, and desired of the king that he would appoint him a time, and he would show the king the interpretation.
Then Daniel went to his house, and made the thing known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions:
that they would desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret; that Daniel and his companions should not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.
Then was the secret revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
Daniel answered, Blessed be the name of God forever and ever; for wisdom and might are his.
He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;
he reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.
I thank you, and praise you, you God of my fathers, who have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we desired of you; for you have made known to us the king’s matter.

Therefore Daniel went in to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon; he went and said thus to him: Don’t destroy the wise men of Babylon; bring me in before the king, and I will show to the king the interpretation.
Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste, and said thus to him, I have found a man of the children of the captivity of Judah, who will make known to the king the interpretation.
The king answered Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, Are you able to make known to me the dream which I have seen, and its interpretation?
Daniel answered before the king, and said, The secret which the king has demanded can neither wise men, enchanters, magicians, nor soothsayers, show to the king;
but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:
as for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter; and he who reveals secrets has made known to you what shall happen.

But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living, but to the intent that the interpretation may be made known to the king, and that you may know the thoughts of your heart.
You, O king, saw, and behold,  a great image. This image, which was mighty, and whose brightness was excellent, stood before you; and its aspect was awesome.
As for this image, its head was of fine gold, its breast and its arms of silver, its belly and its thighs of brass,
its legs of iron, its feet part of iron, and part of clay.
You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces.

Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
This is the dream; and we will tell its interpretation before the king.
You, O king, are king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, and the strength, and the glory;
and wherever the children of men dwell, the animals of the field and the birds of the sky has he given into your hand, and has made you to rule over them all: you are the head of gold.
After you shall arise another kingdom inferior to you; and another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth.
The fourth kingdom shall be strong as iron, because iron breaks in pieces and subdues all things; and as iron that crushes all these, shall it break in pieces and crush.

Whereas you saw the feet and toes, part of potters’ clay, and part of iron, it shall be a divided kingdom; but there shall be in it of the strength of the iron, because you saw the iron mixed with miry clay.
As the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly broken.
Whereas you saw the iron mixed with miry clay, they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men; but they shall not cling to one another, even as iron does not mingle with clay.

In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.

Because you saw that a stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the brass, the clay, the silver, and the gold; the great God has made known to the king what shall happen hereafter: and the dream is certain, and its interpretation sure.
Then the king Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face, and worshiped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an offering and sweet odors to him.
The king answered to Daniel, and said, Of a truth your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, since you have been able to reveal this secret.
Then the king made Daniel great, and gave him many great gifts, and made him to rule over the whole province of Babylon, and to be chief governor over all the wise men of Babylon.
Daniel requested of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, over the affairs of the province of Babylon: but Daniel was in the gate of the king.

footnotes.content: A king who has everything—power, wealth, armies—yet sleep flees from him. Nebuchadnezzar's sleep is troubled not by worry but by a dream the Lord has placed in his heart. Sometimes the Almighty troubles a king's rest not to punish but to prepare him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He gathers all his wise men—magicians, enchanters, sorcerers, all the learned of the kingdom. In his fear, the king calls upon human wisdom first. We do the same when our hearts are troubled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "My spirit is troubled to know the dream." He doesn't just want the dream repeated; he wants to understand what it means. This hunger for understanding is often what the Lord uses to turn a heart toward Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Chaldeans speak in Aramaic—a detail the Lord preserved for us. Notice they promise they can interpret any dream if only he tells it. Confidence born of human skill alone is quick to crumble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nebuchadnezzar refuses to tell the dream. This is his demand: prove your wisdom not by cleverness but by showing you know something only gods could know. His impatience cracks open the lie that human learning is enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He dangles rewards—gifts, riches, great honor. The promise is rich, but notice: it doesn't change the Chaldeans' answer. Earthly reward cannot buy what only heaven can supply.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They try again: "Tell us the dream." Human wisdom, when pressed, retreats to its limits and repeats itself. The wise men know they are at an end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nebuchadnezzar sees through them—they are stalling, buying time in the hope the dream will come back to him. His eye is sharp for deception, even if his heart still trusts in men.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Tell me the dream, and I shall know that you can show me its interpretation." He sets this as the test: if you can do the impossible, I will trust your reading of it. God often lets us demand proof before we believe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Chaldeans confess: no man on earth can do this. No king has ever asked it of any magician or enchanter. They are admitting that human wisdom has a boundary—a merciful admission.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "There is no other who can show it...except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh." Even pagan sorcerers know: what you are asking belongs to heaven, not earth. Trapped between the king's fury and their own limits, they point upward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's anger burns hot. When human wisdom fails us, we often turn to rage. Nebuchadnezzar orders the death of all Babylon's wise men—a decree born of fear and pride together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They sought Daniel and his companions to be slain. The decree spreads its net wide. Daniel was not at the council—but he is caught in the consequence. Sometimes we suffer for others' failures, and that is when faith is most needed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel meets Arioch the guard with counsel and prudence. Notice: he doesn't panic. Even in the shadow of death, Daniel is calm and thoughtful. This is the fruit of a heart that trusts the God of heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why is the decree so urgent?" Daniel asks. By asking wisely, he learns the whole story. A good question, asked in the right spirit, often opens a door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel goes to the king and asks for time—a deadline, a moment to show what he can do. He doesn't boast; he simply asks for an opportunity. Courage speaks quietly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He gathers his companions—Hananiah, Mishael, Azariah. Three friends bound by faith, called by different names in a foreign land, but true to the God of their fathers. We are strongest when we seek God together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "That they would desire mercies...concerning this secret." Daniel does not ask for wisdom first; he asks for mercy. He knows that what they need is grace from the God of heaven. This is the posture of a true seeker.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The secret is revealed in the night—in prayer, in darkness, when human help is far away. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven. The gratitude comes before the interpretation, before any reward. This is the heart of a worshiper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel's prayer opens with praise: "Blessed be the name of God forever and ever; for wisdom and might are his." This is the voice of one who has touched the living God. His words echo through the ages: God alone holds true wisdom and power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings." Daniel sees what the wise men could not—that history itself is in God's hand. Every empire rises and falls by His counsel, not by human cunning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He reveals the deep and secret things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him." In one verse, Daniel names why he can know the dream: the God of heaven is Lord of all mysteries, and darkness holds no secrets from Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel thanks and praises, saying 'you God of my fathers.' He remembers that his God is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—the faithful God through all generations. When we pray, we join a long cloud of witnesses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He goes to Arioch and says: "Don't destroy the wise men; bring me before the king." In his own deliverance, Daniel thinks of others. This is mercy born not of law but of grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Arioch brings Daniel before Nebuchadnezzar with hope rekindled: "I have found a man...who will make known the interpretation." From death's door to the throne room—the Lord can turn a captive's fortune in an instant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king calls him Belteshazzar—his Babylonian name—yet asks if he can truly do this impossible thing. Even kings doubt. Yet Nebuchadnezzar is about to see that the God of captives is greater than all earthly power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel answers plainly: the wise men, enchanters, and magicians cannot do this. He names them all and says no. Before he says what *can* happen, he speaks the truth that all human wisdom has a limit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "But there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets." In one sentence, Daniel moves the king's gaze from earth to heaven. Then he speaks the words Nebuchadnezzar needs to hear: God *has* made known what shall be in the latter days.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter." The king's own wondering mind drew the secret down; God planted the vision there. Often we don't know when God is speaking to us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel refuses to claim this for himself: "This secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have...but to the intent that the interpretation may be made known to the king." True faithfulness gives all glory to God and all purpose to His will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The dream: a great image, mighty and bright, of awesome aspect. This image stands in the palace of the mind—the place where a king makes his decisions. Visions from God often come in forms we must work to understand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Head of fine gold, breast and arms of silver, belly and thighs of brass. The image grows coarser, weaker as it descends. There is a lesson hidden in the metals themselves: the finest kingdoms fade.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Legs of iron, feet part iron and part clay. The image crumbles as it goes down—strong iron mixed with fragile clay. An empire built on strength divided against itself cannot stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A stone cut out without hands strikes the feet and breaks them. Suddenly, in the vision, something enters from outside—not carved by man, not born of the kingdoms, but sent from heaven to do what no earthly hand could do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the metals shatter together and are carried away like chaff. The stone becomes a great mountain filling the whole earth. One blow shatters all human empires; one kingdom—the Lord's—endures forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "This is the dream; and we will tell its interpretation before the king." Daniel moves now from vision to meaning. He speaks as 'we'—Daniel and his friends, or Daniel and the God of heaven. Authority rests not in him alone but in his connection to the Most High.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You, O king, are king of kings...the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, and the strength, and the glory." Here Daniel speaks directly to Nebuchadnezzar's place in history. He is the head of gold—the greatest of the empires to come, yet still only a head, not the whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God has given him the beasts of the field and the birds—dominion over creation itself. Yet even this vast power cannot escape the dream's meaning: he is the first, but not the last.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After Nebuchadnezzar comes another kingdom inferior to him—silver, not gold. Then a third of brass. Empires rise in succession, each with some might, but each less glorious than the one before. Man's glory fades.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fourth kingdom is iron—strong and terrible, crushing all things. Not wisdom or beauty, but iron brute strength. History shows us how raw power can rule when grace grows thin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The feet are iron mixed with miry clay—strength divided and weakened. A kingdom built on iron and clay cannot endure; it crumbles from within. When power divides against itself, it falls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Partly strong, partly broken. The final human kingdom is unstable, unable to hold itself together. This is the condition of earthly rule: always cracking, always coming apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They mingle with the seed of men but do not cling together. The final empire tries to bind itself by intermarriage, by treaty, by alliance—but iron does not cling to clay. No earthly politics can hold what God intends to break.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed." Here is the hope: not in the rise and fall of empires, but in a kingdom from heaven that breaks them all and stands forever. Christ's kingdom is that stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The dream is certain and its interpretation sure. Daniel closes not with his own words but with the seal of heaven: what God has shown is trustworthy. This is our anchor in a world of shifting kingdoms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nebuchadnezzar falls on his face and worships Daniel. A great king humbles himself before a captured youth. Power bends when it touches truth. Yet Daniel knows that all worship belongs to God alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Of a truth your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets." Even a pagan king speaks the name and nature of the living God. His eyes have been opened to reality—not by argument but by the simple power of truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king makes Daniel great, gives him gifts, and sets him to rule over Babylon's wise men. From the shadow of the death decree to the seat of power—the Lord exalted his faithful servant. Yet Daniel's greatness begins not in honor but in humility before God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel requests that his three companions be appointed over Babylon's affairs; he himself sits in the gate. Even in exaltation, he lifts up those who stood with him in prayer. Readers today hear an echo in this faithfulness—the Lord honors those who honor Him and care for their brothers in faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
